title: Muslim Americans combine growing demographic and political visibility with persistent discrimination and a more polarized public image after 9/11
source_unit: Pew Research Center, 25 Years After 9/11, a Portrait of Muslim Americans
geography: United States; U.S. adults and Muslim American adults across identity, generation, nativity and political context

observations.period: May 4-17, 2026 and January 2026 public-opinion surveys; national perceptions of Muslims and Islam

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in Pew public-opinion surveys; exact item-level bases vary

negative_impact.unit: per cent saying Muslims have a very or somewhat negative impact on the country

positive_impact.unit: per cent saying Muslims have a very or somewhat positive impact on the country

less_patriotic.unit: per cent saying Muslims are less patriotic than other Americans

islam_violence.unit: per cent saying Islam encourages violence more than other religions; 76% among Republicans and 29% among Democrats

historical_shift.value: The Islam-violence measure was 25% in March 2002 and ranged from 38% to 52% in later readings, including 45%-52% in the last decade.

observations.method: Pew national public-opinion surveys; the Islam-violence series used telephone surveys from 2002-2015 and the American Trends Panel from 2016-2026.
observations.uncertainty: The measures capture public perceptions rather than Muslims' actual patriotism, social contribution or religious beliefs; question wording, mode changes and partisan composition constrain direct long-run comparison.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults by political affiliation and perceptions of Muslims and Islam.
observations.counterinterpretation: Polarized perceptions may reflect broader partisan sorting and media environments as well as changing views of Muslims specifically; the data do not establish which mechanism dominates.

observations.period: 2026 Muslim American survey; reported support, discrimination and news coverage

denominator.unit: U.S. Muslim adults in Pew survey; exact item-level bases vary

support.unit: per cent saying someone expressed support for them in the past year because they are Muslim

a_lot_of_discrimination.unit: per cent saying there is a lot of discrimination against Muslims in the country

unfair_news.unit: per cent saying news coverage of Islam or Muslims is often unfair

historical_context.value: In the comparable 2017 survey, 49% reported support, 48% a lot of discrimination and 60% unfair TV or movie portrayals; the source also reports earlier 2001, 2007 and 2011 readings.

observations.method: Pew survey of Muslim American adults with historical comparisons to prior Pew Muslim American surveys.
observations.uncertainty: Self-reported support, discrimination and perceived coverage are not a complete incident census and do not identify frequency, perpetrator, institutional remedy or downstream effects.
observations.subgroup: Muslim American adults, with historical comparisons across survey years.
observations.counterinterpretation: Support and discrimination can coexist in the same social environment; the findings do not imply that every Muslim American experiences either condition uniformly.

observations.period: 2000-2026; demographic, congregational and political visibility of Muslim Americans

denominator.unit: Mixed population estimates, mosque counts, FBI reported incidents and congressional membership

population.value: Estimated Muslim population rose from 2.4 million in 2007 to 5.5 million in 2026.

mosques.value: Mosque count rose from about 1,200 in 2000 to about 2,800 in 2020.

hate_crimes.value: FBI recorded 481 anti-Islamic hate-crime incidents in 2001 and 205 in 2025; comparison years include 307 in 2016 and 95 in 2021.

political_visibility.value: There were no Muslim members of Congress in 2001, compared with four and a fifth about to join in the 2026 account; the source also describes the first Muslim mayor of New York City.

observations.method: Pew population estimates and surveys, independent mosque counts, FBI Uniform Crime Reporting data and public-record political representation.
observations.uncertainty: Population and mosque estimates are not a decennial census; FBI counts reflect reported incidents and changing participation and collection systems, including the NIBRS transition, and should not be read as a complete measure of harm.
observations.subgroup: U.S. Muslim population, congregations, reported hate-crime incidents and elected officials.
observations.counterinterpretation: Institutional growth and political visibility may expand capacity and voice without implying that discrimination or public suspicion has receded; the series does not identify causal relationships among these measures.

observations.period: 2017 Muslim American survey; age and nativity differences in discrimination, friendliness and news coverage

denominator.unit: U.S. Muslim adults in 2017 Pew survey; historical subgroup comparison

age_discrimination.value: 53% of Muslims ages 18-40 reported discrimination, compared with 40% of those ages 41 and older.

nativity_discrimination.value: 61% of U.S.-born Muslims reported discrimination, compared with 39% of foreign-born Muslims.

nativity_friendliness.value: 30% of U.S.-born Muslims said American people are generally friendly toward Muslims, compared with 73% of foreign-born Muslims.

nativity_unfair_news.value: 74% of U.S.-born Muslims said news coverage was unfair, compared with 49% of foreign-born Muslims.
nativity_unfair_news.unit: per cent reporting perceived unfair coverage

observations.method: Pew 2017 Muslim American survey subgroup comparisons, included by the 2026 retrospective source.
observations.uncertainty: These are historical cross-sectional subgroup differences, not current 2026 estimates or longitudinal evidence that nativity or age causes the reported experiences.
observations.subgroup: Muslim American adults by age and nativity.
observations.counterinterpretation: Differences may reflect cohort, location, language, immigration selection, racialization or different exposure to U.S. institutions rather than nativity alone.

related_sources.claim: Official Pew retrospective combining Muslim American surveys, public opinion, FBI hate-crime data, population estimates, mosque counts and political representation.

boundary: This record adds a religion, civic identity and political-visibility layer to the cross-source atlas: demographic and institutional growth can coexist with persistent discrimination and polarized public perceptions. It is a mixed data essay, not a complete national discrimination or hate-crime census, a causal analysis of post-9/11 effects, a direct household mobility study or one fully consistent time series across all measures.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Pew source page was reviewed for 2026 public perceptions, Muslim American experiences, historical survey comparisons, FBI hate-crime counts, population and mosque estimates, political representation and subgroup boundaries.
